prompt.adult: In Psalm 1, the person who delights in God's law is compared to what?
prompt.child: Psalm 1 talks about a person who loves God's law. What is that person like?
prompt.teen: Psalm 1 describes someone who delights in God's law. What is that person compared to?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 1:3, what is the one who delights in the law of the LORD likened to?

verses.text: He shall be like a tree Planted by the rivers of water, That brings forth its fruit in its season, Whose leaf also shall not wither; And whatever he does shall prosper.

explanation.adult: Psalm 1:3 opens with a picture from nature. Read the first line of the verse.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 1:3. The first line tells what this person is like, and the rest tells how it grows.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 1:3. The first line gives the picture, and the next lines describe it.
explanation.older: Psalm 1:3 begins with the comparison, then describes where it is planted and how it bears fruit.

teaching.extended_explanation: The verse describes something planted by water that bears fruit in its season and whose leaf does not wither. Look at the very first line.
teaching.takeaway: The one who delights in God's law is like a tree planted by the rivers of water.

prompt.adult: What does David name in the sky?
prompt.child: David looks up and names things in the sky. What does he name?
prompt.teen: When David considers the heavens, what does he name in the sky?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 8:3, what does David name in the sky?

verses.text: When I consider Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, The moon and the stars, which You have ordained,

explanation.adult: Psalm 8:3 tells what David names when he looks up. Read the middle of the verse.
explanation.child: David is looking at the sky in Psalm 8:3. Read what he names there.
explanation.teen: Psalm 8:3 lists what David names in the heavens. Look after “the work of Your fingers.”
explanation.older: Read the middle of Psalm 8:3 for what David names in the sky.

teaching.extended_explanation: David is thinking about the heavens as the work of God's fingers. The next words name what he sees there.
teaching.takeaway: David names the moon and the stars.

review.notes: Sprout stage. NKJV excerpt copied from _sprout_nkjv.json (BibleGateway NKJV). Answer is in the cited verse. Manager B/C review: moved off Psalm 8:1/8:9 (“Your name”). Did not change that answer to “His name,” which Psalm 100:4 would leak. Now Psalm 8:3, “The moon and the stars.”

prompt.adult: According to Psalm 19:1, what do the heavens declare?
prompt.child: Psalm 19 says the sky is telling us something. What do the heavens declare?
prompt.teen: Psalm 19:1 says the heavens are speaking. What do they declare?
prompt.older: In Psalm 19:1, what is it that the heavens declare?

verses.text: The heavens declare the glory of God; And the firmament shows His handiwork.

explanation.adult: Psalm 19:1 gives two parallel lines about the sky. Read the first line.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 19:1. The first part tells what the heavens declare, and the second tells what the sky shows.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 19:1. The first line tells what the heavens declare.
explanation.older: Psalm 19:1 is written in two parallel lines. The first names what the heavens declare.

teaching.extended_explanation: The verse says the sky itself speaks without words. It points to the One who made it. Read the first line closely.
teaching.takeaway: The heavens declare the glory of God.

prompt.adult: In Psalm 23:1, David says the LORD is his what?
prompt.child: Psalm 23 begins by telling who the LORD is to David. What does David call Him?
prompt.teen: In the first line of Psalm 23, what does David call the LORD?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 23:1, what does David declare the LORD to be to him?

verses.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

explanation.adult: Psalm 23:1 is short. Read the first half of the verse.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 23:1. David tells who the LORD is to him, and then says he will not be in need.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 23:1. The first half names what the LORD is to David.
explanation.older: The opening clause of Psalm 23:1 gives the title David uses for the LORD.

teaching.extended_explanation: David tells what the LORD is to him. Read the first half of the verse.

review.notes: Sprout stage. NKJV excerpt copied from _sprout_nkjv.json (BibleGateway NKJV). Answer is in the cited verse. Manager B/C review: rewrote the extended explanation so it no longer almost gives the answer away.

prompt.adult: In Psalm 23, what does David say shall follow him all the days of his life?
prompt.child: David says two things will follow him every day of his life. What are they?
prompt.teen: Psalm 23 ends with David naming what will stay with him his whole life long. What is it?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 23:6, what shall follow David all the days of his life?

verses.text: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me All the days of my life; And I will dwell in the house of the LORD Forever.

explanation.adult: Psalm 23:6 tells what shall follow David all the days of his life. Read the first part of the verse.
explanation.child: Psalm 23:6 says something will follow David his whole life. Read the first part to see what it is.
explanation.teen: The opening of Psalm 23:6 names what will follow David. Read those first words.
explanation.older: Read the first line of Psalm 23:6 for what shall follow David all his days.

teaching.extended_explanation: The last verse of this psalm looks ahead through all of David's days, and then to the house of the LORD. Read the first half for what follows him.
teaching.takeaway: Goodness and mercy shall follow David all the days of his life.

review.notes: Sprout stage. NKJV excerpt copied from _sprout_nkjv.json (BibleGateway NKJV). Answer is in the cited verse. Manager B/C review: moved from Psalm 23:2 (which contains “still waters,” answering psa-0006) to Psalm 23:6. Answer: “Goodness and mercy.”

prompt.adult: In Psalm 46:10, God tells His people to be what, and know that He is God?
prompt.child: In Psalm 46:10, God gives a short command before saying "know that I am God." What does He tell people to be?
prompt.teen: Psalm 46:10 has a short command from God. What does He tell people to be, and know that He is God?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 46:10, what does God call His people to be as they know that He is God?

verses.text: Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!

explanation.adult: Psalm 46:10 begins with a short command. Read the first words of the verse.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 46:10. The first few words tell what God wants people to be.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 46:10. The very first words are the command.
explanation.older: The command appears in the opening words of Psalm 46:10, just before "and know that I am God."

teaching.extended_explanation: This psalm speaks of mountains shaking and nations raging. Then God speaks a calm command at the start of verse 10.
teaching.takeaway: Be still, and know that I am God.

prompt.adult: According to Psalm 100:4, with what should we enter God's gates?
prompt.child: Psalm 100 tells us how to come into God's gates. What should we bring with us?
prompt.teen: Psalm 100:4 says how to come through God's gates. With what should we enter?
prompt.older: In Psalm 100:4, with what are worshipers told to enter the LORD's gates?

verses.text: Enter into His gates with thanksgiving, And into His courts with praise. Be thankful to Him, and bless His name.

explanation.adult: Psalm 100:4 names the gates and the courts. Read what goes with the gates.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 100:4. It tells how to enter the gates and how to enter the courts.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 100:4. The first line tells how to enter His gates.
explanation.older: Psalm 100:4 pairs the gates and the courts, each with its own way of coming in. Note the first line.

teaching.extended_explanation: This verse gives two places, gates and courts, and a way to enter each. The answer goes with the gates in the first line.
teaching.takeaway: We enter God's gates with thanksgiving.

prompt.adult: In Psalm 119:111, why does the psalmist take God's testimonies as his heritage forever?
prompt.child: In Psalm 119:111, the writer says he keeps God's words forever. Why does he keep them?
prompt.teen: Psalm 119:111 says the writer has made God's testimonies his heritage forever. What reason does he give?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 119:111, for what reason has the psalmist taken God's testimonies as a heritage forever?

choices.text: They made him rich and powerful
They are the rejoicing of his heart

verses.text: Your testimonies I have taken as a heritage forever, For they are the rejoicing of my heart.

explanation.adult: Psalm 119:111 gives a reason after the word "For." Read the second line.
explanation.child: Read Psalm 119:111. The second part starts with "For" and tells why.
explanation.teen: Check Psalm 119:111. The reason comes after the word "For."
explanation.older: The second clause of Psalm 119:111, introduced by "For," states the reason.

teaching.extended_explanation: A heritage is something treasured and kept. The second line of the verse tells what God's testimonies do for the writer.
teaching.takeaway: God's testimonies are the rejoicing of the psalmist's heart.
